title: Revoke a Bad Decision Publicly
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Admired Leadership isolates a narrow but high-leverage moment: what a leader does when a decision they made has to be undone. The observed default is quiet replacement — the bad decision is superseded by a new one, with no conversation acknowledging that the first was weak. The author argues this wastes the credibility available in that moment, because revoking the old decision openly, in front of the people it affected, is the act that actually reads as authenticity. The piece is specific about what counts: a mandated policy, a pricing or compensation model, an investment, a strategy that flopped. The claimed return is a shift in how the leader is perceived — not merely courageous and honest, but open-minded, objective, and oriented to the team's interest. The framing throughout is symbolic: because admitting error is rare and costly-looking, doing it publicly projects character and competence at once.
points: The actionable distinction is between silently replacing a failed decision and explicitly revoking it in front of the people it affected — only the second buys credibility.
The author identifies the default behavior precisely: new decisions quietly take center stage while the weak one is never named.
Public revocation is claimed to change the perceived category of the leader, from courageous-and-honest to open-minded and objective about the team's interest.
The piece grants that this takes nerve many leaders cannot find, which is exactly why it functions as a costly and therefore credible signal.
Examples are enumerated concretely — policies, pricing or compensation models, investments, strategies — so the advice cannot be read as applying only to trivial calls.
quotes: Team members respect leaders who own up to their missteps and show themselves to be human in the process. It takes a secure and self-confident leader to acknowledge to others that they have slipped up.

One mistake worth noting for its symbolic value is when the mistake is a faulty decision. On occasion, leaders make decisions that turn out to fail or have unintended negative consequences. The natural tendency for leaders is to endure this bad decision until it can no longer be kept in place.

In most instances, poor choices and decisions simply get corrected by introducing new decisions that replace them. Little conversation is held to acknowledge the weak decision. Instead, the new decision that overrides the old one takes center stage.

At the moment of announcing a new decision going forward, an opportunity exists to significantly enhance a leader’s credibility. Revoking the old decision publicly, in front of those impacted by it, takes nerve and courage many leaders can’t find. But when they do so, credibility rises like a rocket.

The symbolism conveyed by a leader who confesses that a given decision deserves to be blown up and discarded speaks volumes about authenticity and trustworthiness. We don’t view this leader merely as courageous and honest. We also see them as open-minded and objective leaders who are dedicated to doing what’s best for the team.

When a bad decision needs to be rescinded, good leaders don’t miss the opportunity to project their true character and competence. Revoking a poor decision publicly is a ticket to win the hearts and minds of the team.
